item.title: Julien Camirand Lemire (Nord Quantique): One Cavity, One Error-Corrected Qubit
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because Nord Quantique’s demonstration of a fully error‑corrected logical qubit using just one superconducting microwave cavity shows that bosonic codes can deliver quantum error correction without the massive physical‑qubit overhead required by surface‑code architectures. By implementing both GKP and their proprietary “Tesseract” code and reporting an error‑correction gain of more than two‑fold, the team provides a concrete benchmark that complements recent advances from Google and IBM on multi‑qubit logical operations. If the approach scales to larger registers, it could dramatically simplify hardware layouts and accelerate the path toward fault‑tolerant quantum processors, though further work is needed to integrate many such cavities into a coherent architecture.

Julien Camirand Lemire, co-founder and CEO of Nord Quantique, is interviewed by Yuval Boger. Julien discusses Nord Quantique‘s bosonic code approach, which uses microwave photons in superconducting cavities to achieve quantum error correction without large qubit overhead, including their GKP and Tesseract code demonstrations and a quantum error correction gain that has more than doubled […]

item.title: Sandia and Quantinuum Introduce Logical Gate Set Tomography to Map Fault-Tolerant Qubit Noise
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first self‑consistent tomographic reconstruction of an entire universal single‑qubit logical gate set—“Logical GST”—demonstrated on a Steane‑code logical qubit in Quantinuum’s H1‑1 processor. By confirming that error correction largely reduces physical noise to simple Pauli‑stochastic channels while also exposing subtle coherent over‑rotations and non‑Markovian effects, the work provides a crucial diagnostic tool for tightening fault‑tolerance thresholds as hardware scales. The ability to map logical‑level errors directly will help both academia and industry refine control strategies and benchmark next‑generation error‑corrected processors.

Researchers from Sandia National Laboratories and Quantinuum have introduced "Logical GST," a protocol that provides the first self-consistent, full tomographic reconstruction of a universal single-qubit logical gate set. This was implemented on a single logical qubit encoded in the [[7, 1, 3]] Steane code on the Quantinuum System Model H1-1. The study confirmed the assumption that quantum error correction converts complex physical noise into simple, uncorrelated Pauli-stochastic channels, but high-shot emulation revealed small but statistically significant logical non-Markovianity and coherent logical over-rotations. item.title: Quantinuum Chief Scientist Argues Physical Fidelity Trumps Gate Speed in Fault-Tolerant Scaling Race
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article spotlights a pivotal debate in the race toward fault‑tolerant quantum computers: whether ultra‑low error rates or sheer gate speed will drive scalability. By emphasizing Quantinuum’s trapped‑ion platform—whose physical fidelities already eclipse many superconducting chips—the piece underscores how higher fidelity can dramatically shrink the overhead of quantum error correction, a bottleneck that has slowed practical deployments. If Quantinuum meets its 2029 target for faster ion gates, the combination of low errors and competitive speed could reshape industry roadmaps and accelerate the arrival of commercially viable quantum services.

Quantinuum's Chief Scientist, Harry Buhrman, argues that high physical fidelity in quantum gates is more critical than raw gate speed for achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing. He highlights Quantinuum's trapped-ion architecture as superior to superconducting platforms due to its low error rates, which significantly reduce the resources needed for quantum error correction. While trapped-ion systems currently have slower gate speeds, Quantinuum aims to overcome this limitation by 2029 to make its Apollo system commercially competitive. item.title: Forschungszentrum Jülich Demonstrates 6.8-Nanosecond Single-Qubit Gates with > 99.98% Fidelity via Multi-Photon Leakage Suppression
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article showcases a new “R2D” pulse‑shaping technique that pushes single‑qubit gate times down to 6.8 ns while still exceeding 99.98 % fidelity, a combination rarely achieved on superconducting transmons and one that directly tackles the speed‑versus‑leakage trade‑off that has limited previous hardware generations. By suppressing multi‑photon leakage, the work narrows the gap between gate performance and the error thresholds required for fault‑tolerant surface‑code operations, complementing recent advances in microwave‑driven two‑qubit gates and cryogenic control electronics. The results are promising for scaling up quantum processors, but extending the method to multi‑qubit entangling operations will be the next critical hurdle.

Physicists at Forschungszentrum Jülich, RWTH Aachen University, and the University of Cologne have achieved record-breaking 6.8-nanosecond single-qubit gate operations with over 99.98% fidelity on a superconducting transmon processor. Their "R2D" pulse-shaping method effectively suppresses multi-photon leakage, allowing for ultrafast gates while maintaining high fidelity. This advancement, detailed in Nature Communications, marks a significant step in quantum computing, though scaling to multi-qubit systems presents future challenges. By pairing an automated scheduling compiler with dynamical decoupling, IQM pushes the practical limits of error mitigation and highlights how software–hardware co‑design is becoming essential for scaling quantum processors. The result signals a tangible step toward larger, fault‑tolerant machines, though maintaining such coherence under more complex algorithms will remain a key challenge.

IQM Quantum Computers has successfully demonstrated full-chip entanglement across all 54 qubits of its IQM Emerald processor, a significant advancement in quantum computing. This achievement validates full-lattice coherence on commercial hardware, with measured state fidelities exceeding the genuine multipartite entanglement threshold. The company utilized an automated scheduling compiler and dynamical decoupling to achieve this milestone, highlighting both progress and the ongoing challenges in maintaining coherence in quantum systems. item.title: Entanglement diagnostics of stochastic-resetting steady states: theory and measurement on superconducting qubits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that stochastic‑reset protocols can deliberately steer many‑body qubit arrays into exotic nonequilibrium steady states whose entanglement structure is tunable by the reset history—a capability that goes beyond what ordinary unitary dynamics can produce. By deriving closed‑form formulas for small Ising chains and confirming them on an IBM superconducting processor, the authors demonstrate that both entropy‑based and concurrence‑based diagnostics faithfully capture the predicted physics, while a simple depolarizing error model explains the modest loss of concurrence in real hardware. The work opens a practical route to using reset‑driven dynamics for quantum sensing of temporal information (via the Jensen gap/Holevo quantity) and for engineering robust entangled resources that could aid error mitigation or reservoir‑engineering schemes in near‑term devices.

Stochastic resetting drives quantum systems into nonequilibrium stationary states unreachable under uninterrupted unitary evolution, and their entanglement depends on whether the reset history is resolved or averaged over. We study this interplay in the transverse-field Ising chain, deriving closed-form results for two qubits and evaluating chains of up to 12 qubits exactly. In the two-qubit system, these closed-form results show that phase matching between energy eigenstates produces resonances, and their visibility in the stationary state is determined by the symmetry of the reset state. Measurements on an IBM superconducting processor show the entropies evaluated before and after the reset average closely following noiseless predictions with no fitted parameter, while concurrence lies below prediction across most of the hardware measurements. The two diagnostics respond differently because they read different components of the same reconstructed state, and a depolarizing model captures the concurrence suppression with one fitted parameter. The difference between the two entropies, i. e., the Jensen gap of entanglement entropy, equals the Holevo information that a subsystem retains about the time since the last reset. With a Bell-state reset, this information grows with chain length across a half-chain cut over the sizes studied, without visible saturation at the smaller reset probabilities. Since reset times are sampled and recorded classically, the trajectory-averaged entropy, and with it the Jensen gap, is obtained without postselection, in contrast to monitored circuits, where trajectory-resolved entanglement requires sampling exponentially rare measurement records.

item.title: Classical communication over quantum channels: does entanglement help in nature?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article narrows the gap between theory and practice by showing that entangling codewords offers no boost for a broad family of physically relevant channels—including multi‑level amplitude‑damping, dephasing and other phase‑covariant maps—so many real‑world communication links are unlikely to benefit from exotic quantum tricks. It builds on Hastings’ breakthrough that disproved the “no‑advantage” conjecture but goes further by proving a Schur‑weighted block entropy inequality that rules out entanglement gains in low‑dimensional, experimentally accessible settings. For engineers designing quantum‑enhanced classical links, the result is reassuring: they can focus on optimizing conventional coding strategies without worrying about missing a hidden entanglement advantage.

Can entangling codewords across independent uses of a quantum channel improve the rate of classical communication? An old conjecture states that there is no such entanglement advantage for all channels. Although Hastings's result and follow-up works disproved this conjecture, it turns out that enormous dimension is required to construct a channel where entanglement enhances classical communication. This indicates that there might be no entanglement advantage for many physical channels, or for all low dimensional channels. Motivated by recent progress on (generalized) amplitude damping channels, we propose a general Schur-weighted block entropy inequality, and show that there is no entanglement advantage for all phase-covariant channels including multi-level amplitude damping channels, generalized dephasing channels, and damping-dephasing channels. As a by-product, we also recover the recently established result that there is no entanglement advantage for all qubit channels.

item.title: Algebraic strong-to-weak symmetry breaking and partial decodability in the surface code
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that even modest coherent Z‑rotations can drive the standard triangular‑lattice surface code into a new “partially decodable” critical regime, revealing universal scaling laws for decoding fidelity that depend only on the lattice aspect ratio. By mapping the problem to a replica SO(1) sigma model and confirming predictions with large‑scale simulations, the authors connect this behavior to an algebraic strong‑to‑weak symmetry‑breaking phase in a dual Z₂ paramagnet—an insight that bridges quantum error correction with concepts from statistical physics. The results suggest that realistic coherent noise may demand decoding strategies beyond conventional Pauli‑frame methods, highlighting both a fresh diagnostic tool for hardware engineers and a cautionary note for fault‑tolerance thresholds built on purely stochastic error models.

Coherent noise can give rise to unconventional regimes of quantum information recovery and mixed-state order. We study these phenomena in two settings related by Wegner duality: the triangular-lattice surface code subject to single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ rotations followed by syndrome measurements, and a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ paramagnet subject to strongly symmetric decoherence. Increasing the rotation angle drives a transition from a decodable phase to a \emph{partially decodable} critical phase in the code, and from a strongly symmetric phase to a phase with \emph{algebraic} $\mathbb{Z}_2$ strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) in the dual paramagnet. We develop a common description of these phenomena in terms of a weakly coupled $\mathrm{SO}(n)$ nonlinear sigma model in the replica limit $n\to1$. Taking this replica limit analytically, we derive universal signatures of the critical phase: an optimal Pauli decoding fidelity that approaches a universal function of the system's aspect ratio in the thermodynamic limit, and a dual fidelity correlator that decays as a universal power law. These observables relate to correlations of twist operators in the sigma model description. Large-scale numerical simulations confirm these analytical predictions. We also argue that the algebraic SWSSB phase cannot be realized by any Pauli dephasing channel acting on the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ paramagnet. We probe this "non-classical" character through the output state's sensitivity to well-separated $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ fluxes inserted in the initial state, which reveals persistent coherence between distinct $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ charge trajectories at long distances.

item.title: Grow, Compress, and Perturb: A Hybrid Quantum-Classical Pathway to Scalable Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces VULCAN, a gradient‑free, layered VQE framework that slashes the operator pool size by up to an order of magnitude and eliminates costly Hamiltonian‑gradient measurements, directly tackling one of the biggest bottlenecks in scalable quantum chemistry. By coupling a grow‑then‑compress ansatz construction with a stochastic Epstein‑Nesbet perturbative correction, the authors demonstrate chemical accuracy on systems as large as 32 logical qubits while using only a fraction of the measurement budget required by ADAPT‑VQE. If these techniques translate to near‑term hardware, they could accelerate the path toward practical quantum simulations of medium‑size molecules without prohibitive circuit depth or sampling overhead.

While Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) variants are among leading candidates for electronic structure calculations on quantum computers, gradient-based operator selection limits their scalability. To solve this, we introduce the Hamiltonian-gradient-free VULCAN (Variational Upbuilding, Layered Compression, Adaptive N-body perturbation) layered VQE framework. Our method dynamically generates ansatz operators using Variational Double Bracket Flow (VDBF) equations. Combined with a linearly scaling minimal complete pool, it creates a pool 4-12 times smaller than QEB (Qubit-Excitation-Based) pools. By appending entire layers simultaneously, Hamiltonian gradient measurements are completely eliminated. Circuit depth is managed via a grow-then-compress scheme using efficient state-overlap measurements, and qubit requirements are reduced by projecting the Hamiltonian onto a dominant-determinant subspace. Using high-performance emulation up to 32 logical qubits, we achieve chemical accuracy at just 5-20% of the measurement cost of batched ADAPT-VQE for hydrogen chains, BeH2 and H2O. For the 32-qubit C3H6, where batched ADAPT-VQE does not reach chemical accuracy, a single VULCAN layer combined with a GPU-accelerated stochastic Epstein-Nesbet (ENPT2) correction does. This stochastic ENPT2 post-processing step enables early termination at chemical accuracy.

item.title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a “neural triage” decoder that combines syndrome consistency checks with a lightweight neural message‑passing network, delivering near‑optimal error‑correction accuracy for ultra‑high‑rate qLDPC codes while cutting decoding latency by one to two orders of magnitude. The breakthrough matters because high‑rate qLDPC codes are among the most promising routes to dramatically reduce the physical qubit overhead required for fault‑tolerant quantum computers, yet their practical adoption has been hampered by slow, computationally intensive decoders. By showing that machine‑learning can be deployed adaptively—only invoking deeper neural processing when needed—the work bridges recent advances in neural belief‑propagation decoders with the real‑time demands of emerging quantum hardware. Readers should note that while the results are impressive for blocks of a few hundred logical qubits, scaling to larger distances and integrating the decoder into actual control stacks will be the next critical steps.

Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

item.title: Fault-Tolerant Heisenberg-Limited Quantum Metrology with Bosonic Probes
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows how to retain Heisenberg‑limited precision in bosonic sensors even when dephasing and circuit‑level errors are present, by embedding the probe in a distance‑d error‑correcting code that suppresses logical failures to order p^{(d+1)/2}. It bridges two fast‑moving fronts—bosonic quantum error correction (e.g., cat and GKP codes) and fault‑tolerant quantum metrology—demonstrating NT² Fisher information with a realistic photon‑number budget, something that non‑fault‑tolerant schemes cannot achieve over long interrogation times. The result points toward practical, high‑sensitivity devices such as optical clocks or force detectors, while noting that the advantage hinges on sufficiently low residual signals and the ability to implement repeated parity checks and resets.

Quantum sensors have been shown to enable more precise measurements than classical sensors. By using entanglement and coherent evolution, the estimation error can be made to scale better in interrogation time, photon count, and other resources, achieving Heisenberg-limited scaling. However, environmental noise and hardware errors typically destroy the coherence of the sensitive quantum states. This motivates the use of fault-tolerant techniques to create more robust quantum sensing protocols. Such fault-tolerant quantum sensing approaches have been shown to enhance sensitivity for qubit systems, but many practical sensors require bosonic probes. In this paper, we propose a fault-tolerant protocol using bosons to estimate displacements in the presence of dephasing noise. We construct an optimal error-correcting code under a mean photon-number constraint. Controlled displacements couple the probe to a repetition-encoded qubit register, while repeated boson-parity measurements and resets remove probe noise without erasing the stored logical phase. Under circuit-level bit-flip noise, a distance-$d$ code suppresses logical failures to order $p^{(d+1)/2}$. We show that, for a decay rate $γ_A$, a total sensing time $T$ and a mean photon number budget $N$, and for sufficiently small residual signals, the Fisher information scales as $NT^2$ over interrogation times of order $γ_A^{-(d+1)/2}$. This is a significant improvement over the non-fault-tolerant approach that achieves Heisenberg scaling only for a total time $\mathcal O(γ_A^{-1})$.

item.title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article matters because it untangles the often‑confused ways that image data can be mapped onto quantum states, clarifying when amplitude encoding truly offers a computational advantage versus when full readout remains classically costly. By linking singular‑value decomposition to entanglement structure and demonstrating how even a single QAOA layer can reshape the energy landscape for a tiny segmentation task, it provides concrete guidance for designing near‑term quantum vision pipelines on hardware such as IBM’s and IQM’s devices. The work also warns that modest quantum improvements may still favor suboptimal labelings, underscoring the need for careful measurement and decoding strategies before practical imaging applications can be realized.

An algebraic correspondence between an imaging model and a quantum state does not specify a computational method: input access, measurement and decoding determine what can be returned. This exposition develops four distinctions for computational-imaging and engineering readers. It separates amplitude encodings of input values from encodings of complete candidate labelings, explaining why amplitude storage does not provide full-array readout. Complex-field interference motivates unknown-phase inference: complementary measurements resolve ambiguities that local Fisher information alone does not detect. Reshaping joint amplitudes into a matrix connects singular-value decomposition to pure-state entanglement, while distinguishing Schmidt rank from conditions for efficient classical simulation. In a four-pixel segmentation, an objective becomes a cost operator and a sampling circuit. One layer of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) lowers mean energy from $1.675$ to $0.686$ relative to uniform sampling, yet makes a nonoptimal labeling more probable than the optimum 0.484 versus 0.365. Archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable local boundary decision. Low-rank state reconstruction and selected quantum algorithms connect these distinctions to an end-to-end resource account. The derivations and reproducible numerical references assume complex linear algebra and probability, without prior quantum mechanics. The accompanying Seeing Amplitudes browser laboratory supports interactive exploration; the article remains self-contained and connects each representation to the estimate or decision it permits and the resources that output requires.

item.title: High-Fidelity Universal Quantum Gates in a Cryogenic Atom Array
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that cryogenic operation can bring neutral‑atom platforms into the same fidelity regime as the best room‑temperature systems, achieving single‑qubit gates at 99.970 % and two‑qubit entangling gates above 99.7 %. By using a direct single‑photon Rydberg transition, the authors avoid the scattering and light‑shift errors that have limited previous tweezer arrays, and their error analysis shows that atomic motion—not fundamental Rydberg decay—is now the dominant source of infidelity. The work therefore opens a clear path to surpassing current gate‑error thresholds for fault‑tolerant quantum computing simply by improving cooling, positioning cryogenic atom arrays as a strong contender for scalable quantum processors.

Neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays have emerged as a leading platform for quantum information processing. The fidelity of entangling gates mediated by Rydberg interactions has improved rapidly and is increasingly constrained by blackbody-radiation-induced transitions, which shorten Rydberg lifetimes and create contaminant states that can cause correlated errors. Cryogenic environments can suppress these transition rates by more than an order of magnitude. However, realizing a universal gate set in such an environment has remained an outstanding challenge. Here, we demonstrate a universal quantum gate set in a cryogenic $^{133}$Cs atom array, with a single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.970(2)% and a raw two-qubit entangling-gate fidelity of 99.76(8)%, within the range of leading room-temperature implementations. The entangling gate uses direct single-photon coupling between the electronic ground state and a Rydberg $P$ state, avoiding scattering and light shifts associated with two-photon coupling. The gate operates at a modest Rabi frequency of $2π\times4.3$ MHz. The measured fidelity agrees with our error model dominated by atomic motion, indicating a straightforward route to higher fidelity through improved cooling, while the fundamental error contribution from Rydberg decay is below $3\times10^{-4}$. These results establish a path to entangling-gate fidelities substantially beyond the current state of the art through cryogenic suppression of Rydberg decay, reducing the overhead for fault-tolerant computation.
